title: MDT-guided language-model reasoning for spinal infection diagnosis
abstract: Abstract Spinal infection is a destructive vertebral disorder in which delayed recognition can permit neurological injury, deformity and systemic disease. Before definitive sampling, clinicians must reconcile disease course, laboratory tests and imaging; among infected patients, distinguishing tuberculous from non-tuberculous disease creates further uncertainty. Large language models could organize this dispersed evidence, but whether structured evidence organization improves diagnostic decisions—and how clinicians respond to its advice—remains uncertain. We developed an MDT-guided workflow: complementary evidence synthesis for infection identification, and source-specific MDT review with conflict reconciliation for tuberculous-aetiology differentiation. In two retrospective centre-specific cohorts, three locally deployed open-weight models were compared with a matched minimal zero-shot baseline on the same patient record, model and clinical question. We then examined clinician decisions in a paired multi-reader, multi-case reader study using fixed MDT-guided AI advice. For infection identification, balanced accuracy increased in all six model-by-centre comparisons, with mean differences of 3.63 percentage points at Centre A and 1.48 percentage points at Centre B. This pattern did not extend to tuberculous-aetiology differentiation, which showed a sensitivity–specificity trade-off and mean balanced-accuracy differences of -5.48 and − 5.40 percentage points. In the reader study, five clinicians made 1,716 matched reader–case–decision assessments; accuracy was 92.1% with fixed AI advice and 89.1% without advice (difference, 3.03 percentage points; fixed-reader case-bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 1.47 to 4.55), with 93 incorrect-to-correct and 41 correct-to-incorrect transitions. Structured MDT-guided reasoning consistently improved broad infection recognition across models and centres, whereas its benefit did not extend to tuberculous-aetiology differentiation. In the reader study, fixed AI advice produced a net improvement in clinicians’ diagnostic accuracy. These findings highlight the task-specific value and limitations of structured language-model reasoning in clinical decision support.

title: A Hybrid Complex Quantum U-Net for Enhanced Medical Polyp Image Segmentation
abstract: Abstract In this work, a hybrid segmentation architecture is proposed that integrates real, complex, and quantum computation within a U-Net framework. The model combines a ResNet-50 encoder for initial feature extraction, a complex-valued bottleneck convolutional block to preserve phase and amplitude information, and a quantum variational layer with eight qubits to encode global statistics derived from complex activations. The proposed model is evaluated on a polyp segmentation task using the PolipSet, Kvasir-SEG, and CVC-ClinicDB datasets, with direct baseline comparisons against a pretrained U-Net and SegFormer reported on PolipSet. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid complex--quantum U-Net achieves the best PolipSet performance among the compared models, with mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 79.36\,\%, while also obtaining 78.29\,\% on Kvasir-SEG and 85.07\,\% on CVC-ClinicDB; the corresponding Dice coefficients are 88.38\,\%, 87.51\,\%, and 91.63\,\%, respectively. On PolipSet, these values outperform baselines such as Attention U-Net with ResNet-50 (IoU 75.93\,\%, Dice 82.94\,\%) and SegFormer (IoU 72.97\,\%, Dice 80.86\,\%). These findings highlight the potential of integrating complex-valued and quantum layers within deep learning pipelines for medical image analysis.

title: Evaluation of Bone Mineral Density in Type II Diabetic and Nondiabetic Individuals in a Mandibular Load-Bearing Region: A Pilot Study
abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate and compare the Bone mineral density (BMD) of the mandibular first molar area in patients with type II diabetes mellitus (T2DM) compared with nondiabetic subjects by using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), and its possible use in pre-implant treatment planning. Materials and Methods A prospective cross-sectional pilot study was conducted in 32 subjects, including 16 with T2DM and 16 systemically healthy controls. CBCT scans were obtained using standardised imaging parameters. Assessment of bone density was done by measuring greyscale values (GVs) in three regions of interest within the mandibular first molar region. These include the crestal bone, 2mm apical to the crest and basal trabecular bone. The mean grey scale values for both groups were compared using appropriate statistical tests, with p < 0.05 considered significant. Glycaemic status will be assessed by measuring Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) levels. Results The diabetic group demonstrated significantly lower mean BMD than the nondiabetic group across all assessed regions (p < 0.005). Age-wise distribution revealed a higher proportion of diabetic patients in the 55–65 years group (62.5%) than in the nondiabetic group (43.75%), indicating a significant association with advancing age (p < 0.005). Statistical analysis was conducted using descriptive and inferential statistics, particularly the chi-square test and Student’s unpaired t-test. The tools utilised in statistical analysis were SPSS 27.0 and GraphPad Prism 7.0. Significance level (p<0.05). Conclusion Type II diabetes mellitus is associated with reduced bone density in the mandibular first molar region, as assessed by grayscale values on cone-beam computed tomography. Site-specific evaluation of bone quality before implant placement may improve treatment planning and assist in recognising patients who require modified surgical protocols. Clinical Significance A comprehensive implant site assessment supports predictive treatment planning, enabling customised implant protocols that improve prosthetic stability. Ongoing monitoring of glycaemic impacts aids effective risk stratification and helps develop evidence-based guidelines.

title: Frame-Based Stereotactic Surgery for a Deep-Seated Brain Cavernoma: A Case Report and Technical Video
abstract: Abstract Background Cerebral cavernomas are the second most common vascular malformation of the central nervous system. While microsurgical excision is standard for accessible symptomatic lesions, stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is preferred for deep-seated or inaccessible cavernomas due to the higher complication risk of open resection, despite carrying its own risks of delayed hemorrhage and radiation-induced injury. Frame-based stereotactic surgical excision may combine the targeting precision of SRS with the immediate efficacy of surgical resection while avoiding radiation exposure. Case Presentation: A 25-year-old female presented with a history of headache, photophobia, blurred vision, and intermittent vomiting. Examination revealed left lateral gaze limitation and bilateral papilledema. MRI demonstrated a 15×20×24 mm intra-axial lesion in the left thalamic region extending to the left cerebral peduncle, causing obstructive hydrocephalus, initially favored as glioma. After endoscopic third ventriculostomy and an inconclusive endoscopic biopsy, stereotactic partial excision was performed using a novel 3D-printed stereotactic frame. Intraoperative findings and histopathology confirmed cavernoma rather than glioma. The procedure was uneventful, with no hemorrhage on postoperative imaging, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day two with an intact neurological examination. Conclusion Frame-based stereotactic surgical excision using this novel low-cost stereotactic system enabled safe, precise debulking of a deep-seated, rare thalamic-peduncular cavernoma, achieving diagnostic confirmation and symptomatic mass-effect reduction without complications. This approach may offer a viable alternative for deep, eloquently located cavernomas where open microsurgery carries excessive risk and SRS risks incomplete treatment and radiation side effects, warranting further evaluation in larger case series.

title: MRI Radiomics for Survival Stratification in Glioblastoma: Benchmarking Against Clinical Variables in a Retrospective Observational Study of the UPENN-GBM Cohort
abstract: Abstract Background Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults and exhibits substantial biological heterogeneity not fully captured by conventional clinical and molecular prognostic factors. MRI radiomics has emerged as a promising approach for deriving quantitative imaging biomarkers associated with patient outcomes. This study aimed to compare conventional clinical survival modeling with MRI radiomics-based machine learning for survival stratification in a public glioblastoma cohort. Methods This retrospective study included 230 patients with glioblastoma from the UPENN-GBM dataset. Clinical variables included age, sex, Karnofsky Performance Status, MGMT promoter status, and IDH1 mutation status. A total of 144 MRI radiomic features were extracted and reduced to 61 after preprocessing and feature selection. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was developed using clinical variables, while a Random Survival Forest (RSF) model was trained using radiomic features. Model performance was assessed using the concordance index (C-index), and survival stratification was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier analysis. Results The clinical Cox model demonstrated moderate prognostic performance (C-index 0.635). Increasing age was associated with worse survival, while IDH1 mutation and MGMT promoter positivity showed favorable survival trends. The radiomics RSF model achieved comparable prognostic discrimination (C-index 0.653) and stratified patients into high-risk and low-risk groups. Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significant survival separation between risk groups (log-rank p < 0.001). Conclusions MRI radiomics-based machine learning enabled meaningful survival stratification in glioblastoma and provided complementary prognostic information alongside conventional clinical variables. Further external validation is required before clinical implementation. Trial registration Not applicable.

title: Attention-Based Deep learning Network for automatic detection of Microsatellite Instability in endoscopy images
abstract: Abstract Background Microsatellite instability (MSI) is a clinically relevant biomarker in colorectal cancer (CRC). In this study, we employed a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) model to differentiate between MSI and microsatellite-stable (MSS) status using endoscopic images. Methods A pathology-proven dataset was constructed from 986 colonoscopy images of 176 patients with CRC. The images were partitioned into training, validation, and test sets. Attention-based ResNet-50 and MobileNet-V2 DCNN architectures were trained and evaluated for their discriminatory performance. The area under the curve (AUC) was used as the primary performance metric, supplemented by accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and precision. Results In the test cohort, the MobileNet-SE model achieved the best performance, with an AUC of 0.874 (95% CI: 0.852–0.896), a precision of 0.830 (95% CI: 0.787–0.863), a sensitivity of 0.714 (95% CI: 0.670–0.754), a specificity of 0.852 (95% CI: 0.815–0.882), and an accuracy of 0.782 (95% CI: 0.754–0.808). Conclusions These findings underscore the clinical utility of endoscopic images in MSI screening and establish a benchmark for an optimal MSI prediction model.

Results In the test cohort, the MobileNet-SE model achieved the best performance, with an AUC of 0.874 (95% CI: 0.852–0.896), a precision of 0.830 (95% CI: 0.787–0.863), a sensitivity of 0.714 (95% CI: 0.670–0.754), a specificity of 0.852 (95% CI: 0.815–0.882), and an accuracy of 0.782 (95% CI: 0.754–0.808). Conclusions These findings underscore the clinical utility of endoscopic images in MSI screening and establish a benchmark for an optimal MSI prediction model.

title: Dynamic Changes in the Vertebral Artery–Subclavian Artery Bifurcation Angle During Cervical Positioning: A Prospective 3D TOF-MRA Study and Implications for Transradial Neurointervention
abstract: Abstract Background: The transradial approach (TRA) is increasingly used for posterior circulation neuroendovascular procedures; however, catheterization of the vertebral artery (VA) may be difficult in patients with an acute VA–subclavian artery (SCA) bifurcation angle. Although cervical positioning is often used to facilitate catheter navigation, its effect on the VA–SCA bifurcation angle has not been quantitatively investigated. This study aimed to evaluate the positional changes in the VA–SCA bifurcation angle using time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA). Methods: In this prospective single-center study, participants underwent time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography in five cervical positions: neutral, 45° right rotation, 45° left rotation, maximal flexion, and maximal extension. The VA–SCA bifurcation angle was measured on coronal multiplanar reconstruction images. Changes relative to the neutral position were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Results: After exclusion of patients with VA occlusion or anatomical variants, a total of 81 right and 75 left VA were analyzed. Cervical flexion significantly decreased the VA–SCA bifurcation angle (right: −8.06°, P < 0.001; left: −3.95°, P = 0.005), whereas cervical extension significantly increased the angle (right: 6.18°, P < 0.001; left: 6.60°, P < 0.001). Cervical rotation produced no significant changes. Conclusions: Cervical flexion decreased, whereas cervical extension increased, the VA–SCA bifurcation angle bilaterally. These positional changes may influence VA accessibility during transradial neuroendovascular procedures. Cervical extension is a simple, cost-free, and readily applicable maneuver that may facilitate VA catheterization in selected patients.

title: Impact of Three-Dimensional Computed Tomography Reconstruction on Clinical Decision-Making in Revisional Bariatric Surgery
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Revisional bariatric surgery is increasingly common because of weight regain, insufficient weight loss, and postoperative anatomical complications, but conventional imaging often fails to provide comprehensive anatomical characterization. Three-dimensional (3D) computed tomography (CT)-based modeling may improve anatomical evaluation and surgical planning, but its impact on clinical decision-making remains insufficiently explored. Methods This retrospective, cross-sectional study included 40 consecutive patients referred for revisional bariatric evaluation between January 2021 and December 2024 at a tertiary referral center. All patients underwent standardized CT acquisition, 3D reconstruction, and gastric volumetric analysis, and were classified into a surgical group (n = 28) or a conservative management group (n = 12) after multidisciplinary assessment. The primary outcome was change in therapeutic management after 3D evaluation; secondary outcomes included weight-loss results, detection of anatomical abnormalities, gastric volumetry, and interobserver reproducibility. Results 3D modeling changed therapeutic decision-making in 42.5% of cases. Surgical plans were cancelled in 20.0% of patients, and 22.5% were reclassified for revisional surgery after 3D anatomical assessment. Anatomical abnormalities were identified in 75.0% of patients, including sleeve dilation (35.0%), intrathoracic gastric migration (15.0%), internal hernias (12.0%), and complex fistulas (8.0%). Gastric volumetry correlated strongly with weight-loss outcomes (r = 0.78, p < 0.001). Patients undergoing revisional surgery achieved significantly greater total weight loss than those managed conservatively (65.0% vs. 12.0%). Interobserver agreement for volumetric measurements was excellent (ICC = 0.96). Conclusion CT-based 3D modeling significantly influenced therapeutic decision-making in revisional bariatric surgery by improving anatomical characterization, identifying clinically relevant abnormalities, and supporting patient selection. These findings support 3D reconstruction as an adjunct in the multidisciplinary evaluation of revisional bariatric patients and warrant validation in prospective multicenter studies.

title: Texture-driven radiomics from longitudinal contrast-enhanced CT predicts short-term immunotherapy response in lung cancer: A retrospective cohort study
abstract: Abstract Background Radiomic prediction of immunotherapy response has been widely reported, yet the nature and localization of the predictive signal remain unclear. We aimed to determine whether longitudinal delta-radiomics (change between serial scans) predicts short-term response in lung cancer, and to dissect the signal by benchmarking against pre-treatment and clinical models, separating texture from shape contributions, and localizing it across intratumoral and peritumoral compartments, and relating it to survival. Methods In a single-center cohort of 156 lung cancer patients receiving first-line immunotherapy, baseline and interim contrast-enhanced CT scans were analyzed. We extracted 1688 radiomic features from intratumoral, peritumoral (3/5/8/10-pixel shells), and combined ROIs, and computed delta features. Short-term response (RECIST 1.1) was modeled using stratified 5-fold cross-validation with all feature selection (univariate filtering, correlation pruning, LASSO) performed inside each training fold. Performance was evaluated by pooled out-of-fold AUC (mean over 5 seeds; 2000-sample bootstrap 95% CI). PFS and OS were assessed by C-index, Kaplan–Meier, and Cox models on cross-validation-averaged risk scores. Results Pre-treatment radiomics was uninformative across all ROIs (AUC 0.48–0.54), as were clinical variables (AUC 0.45). Intratumoral delta-radiomics predicted response with AUC 0.78 (95% CI 0.70–0.85). The signal was texture-driven: texture-only delta reproduced full performance (AUC 0.78), with five of six retained features being texture-based. The effect was consistent across all ROIs and peritumoral distances (AUC 0.74–0.78), and adding clinical, peritumoral, or multi-ROI features provided no improvement. The delta score modestly stratified PFS (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.15–2.39; log-rank p = 0.006; C-index 0.56) but was not associated with OS (p = 0.28); prognostic signal resided specifically in intratumoral-containing ROIs. Conclusions The predictive information in serial CT is texture-driven, intratumoral, and exists only as change — it is not a restatement of tumor shrinkage, does not require peritumoral sampling, and is absent from static pre-treatment imaging. Longitudinal radiomics functions as an early response surrogate that partially tracks progression but does not predict overall survival.

title: Prediction of non-surgical spinal decompression efficacy in lumbar disc herniation patients is based on pre-treatment paravertebral muscle MRI radiomics and clinical factors in a two-center study with external validation.
abstract: Abstract Purpose To develop and validate a predictive model combining pretreatment axial lumbar MRI radiomic features of paravertebral muscles with clinical factors for assessing treatment response to the Non-surgical Spinal Decompression System (SDS) in patients with lumbar disc herniation (LDH). Methods This retrospective dual-center study included 766 LDH patients who underwent SDS. Radiomic features were extracted from segmented multifidus, erector spinae, and psoas major muscles on axial MRI. Six data modalities were constructed and compared using five machine-learning algorithms, with evaluation via five-fold cross-validation and an independent external cohort. Key features were selected by LASSO regression. Model discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility were assessed by ROC curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. SHAP was applied to quantify feature contributions. Results LASSO selected 11 nonzero-coefficient predictors (4 clinical variables, 7 radiomic features). Random forest was the optimal algorithm. The combined clinical-radiomic model achieved internal and external validation AUCs of 0.879 ± 0.039 and 0.835 ± 0.038, significantly outperforming the clinical-only and all single-modality models ( P < 0.05). SHAP showed clinical variables accounted for 53.8% of predictive contribution, with age as the strongest feature. Calibration was good (Hosmer-Lemeshow P > 0.05), and decision curve analysis confirmed positive net benefit across a wide threshold range (0.05–0.85). Conclusion The combined clinical-radiomic model demonstrates good predictive performance for SDS outcomes in LDH patients and holds promise as a clinically useful decision-support tool.

title: Spondylodiscitis due to Stenotrophomonas maltophilia after endoscopic spine surgery: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background. Infection after endoscopic spine surgery is rare, but without timely diagnosis and treatment it can cause severe vertebral destruction. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an intrinsically multidrug-resistant, non-fermenting gram-negative bacillus and an exceptionally rare cause of spinal infection. Case presentation. We report a 54-year-old immunocompetent woman who underwent interlaminar endoscopic discectomy for a right L4–L5 disc herniation. Mechanical low back pain began on postoperative day 3 without fever. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on day 52 demonstrated L4–L5 spondylodiscitis. A positive interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) led to a presumptive diagnosis of spinal tuberculosis treated with a 2RHZE/10RHE regimen, followed by empirical meropenem plus vancomycin; both failed. By day 87, imaging showed osteolysis of the inferior endplate of L4, and the Spinal Instability Spondylodiscitis Score (SISS) was 7, indicating potential instability. The patient underwent posterior L2–S1 instrumentation with L4–L5 debridement. Intraoperative cultures grew S. maltophilia , whereas tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and culture were negative. She received combination levofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for six weeks. At 18 months she was pain-free with stable imaging, and the instrumentation was removed. Conclusions. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of S. maltophilia spondylodiscitis after endoscopic spine surgery. Early mechanical back pain after endoscopic discectomy - even without fever or leukocytosis - should raise suspicion for infection, and specimens for culture should be obtained before empirical antibiotic therapy is started.

title: Individualized Adjuvant Chemotherapy Guided by Pharmacogenomic Testing in a 14-Year-Old with Undifferentiated Embryonal Sarcoma of the Liver
abstract: Abstract Background Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver (UESL) is a rare, aggressive mesenchymal tumor in children, with historically poor prognosis. No standardized adjuvant chemotherapy exists. Pharmacogenomic testing can individualize treatment by predicting drug efficacy and toxicity based on genetic polymorphisms, but its application in UESL has not been reported. Case presentation We report a 14-year-old male presenting with right upper quadrant pain and fever. Imaging revealed a large mixed cystic-solid mass in the right hepatic lobe. He underwent R0 right hemihepatectomy. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirmed UESL with a Ki-67 index of 40%. Postoperative multigene pharmacogenomic testing (84-gene panel) identified key polymorphisms in TP53, ABCB1, and ERCC1, which guided selection of an individualized adjuvant chemotherapy regimen (VDC/IE: vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide, etoposide). The patient completed six cycles without dose reduction or delay, experiencing only grade 1–2 myelosuppression. At 36 months postoperatively, imaging showed no recurrence or metastasis, and the patient had returned to all normal activities. Conclusions This is the first report of systematic multigene pharmacogenomic testing to guide adjuvant chemotherapy in UESL. The patient achieved 36-month disease-free survival with favorable tolerability, a result comparable to or better than historical outcomes with empirical therapy. This case supports the integration of pharmacogenomic testing into individualized treatment strategies for rare sarcomas. Clinical trial number: not applicable.

title: Cone-Beam CT–Guided Thin Linear EBUS Bronchoscopic Biopsy of a Non- Peripheral Lung Nodule: Highlighting the Effect of Bronchoscopic Tools on CT-to-Body Divergence: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Accurate bronchoscopic biopsy of non-peripheral pulmonary nodules adjacent to proximal segmental airways remains challenging. Such lesions lie beyond the reach of standard endobronchial ultrasound transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) and resist accurate bronchoscope angulation in proximal, less flexible bronchi. Case presentation: A 43-year-old non-smoking male was referred for biopsy of an incidentally found 16-mm solid right upper lobe nodule located adjacent to the second subsegmental branch (RB3b). The procedure was performed under general anaesthesia using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)–guided thin linear EBUS bronchoscopy (UCP190F, Olympus; 5.9-mm distal diameter). Intraprocedural CBCT acquisition enabled nodule segmentation and biopsy pathway planning overlaid on augmented fluoroscopy. Real-time ultrasound confirmed lesion localisation. During close-range bronchoscope manipulation, articulation of the bronchoscope tip caused reproducible displacement of the lesion relative to the augmented fluoroscopic target — a phenomenon we term bronchoscope- or tool-induced divergence, distinct from the established concept of CT-to-body divergence. Fine-needle aspiration under simultaneous ultrasound and augmented fluoroscopic guidance, with rapid on-site cytology, confirmed lesional material. Three cryobiopsies were then obtained using a 1.1-mm cryoprobe (Erbe, Tübingen) via the working channel in a wedged, stabilised position. The patient was discharged the same day; histopathology confirmed a typical carcinoid tumour. Conclusions: CBCT-guided bronchoscopy using a thin linear EBUS bronchoscope is feasible for non-peripheral lung nodules in anatomically challenging locations. Awareness of bronchoscope- and tool-induced divergence is clinically relevant and should be considered alongside CT-to-body divergence when targeting accuracy is suboptimal, particularly in proximal airways.

title: Prenatal Diagnosis and Genetic Etiology of Fetal Polycystic Kidney Disease: A Single-Center Retrospective Study of 147 Cases in Yunnan Province, Southwest China
abstract: Abstract Background Fetal polycystic kidney disease (FPDK) is a common ultrasound finding, but its genetic causes vary widely, and data from Yunnan Province are scarce. We aimed to fill this gap by systematically testing a large local cohort. Methods We reviewed 147 FPDK cases seen at our center in Yunnan between 2020 and 2024. All had karyotyping and CNV-seq as first-line tests. Families who tested negative on both were offered trio whole-exome sequencing (trio-WES). Outcomes came from medical records or phone calls. Results Karyotyping detected 18 chromosomal abnormalities (12.2%) mostly trisomy 21 (n = 10), trisomy 13 (n = 3), trisomy 18 (n = 1), 45,X (n = 1), and 47,XXY (n = 1) plus two structural rearrangements. CNV-seq identified isolated pathogenic CNVs in 14 cases (9.5%), ten of which (71.4%) were 17q12 deletions involving HNF1B. Among 32 families who went on to trio-WES, we identified diagnostic single gene variants in 19 (59.4% of those tested, 12.9% overall). The main culprits were PKD1 (n = 6), PKHD1 (n = 4), BBS2 (n = 2), and one each of BBS7 , TMEM67 , TMEM237 , NEK8 , VHL , HNF1B , HDAC8 , CELSR1 , BUB1B , and GRIN1 . All told, we found a genetic cause in 51 of 147 cases (34.7%). Of these, 44 families (86.3%) chose to terminate. Conclusions In this Yunnan cohort, trisomy 21, 17q12 deletion, and PKHD1 / PKD1 mutations were the leading causes. A two-step approach parallel karyotyping and CNV-seq first, then trio-WES for negatives greatly improves detection and gives families essential information for decision‑making. These results offer much needed regional data for prenatal counseling in Yunnan and surrounding areas.

title: Multidisciplinary decision-making in the management of recurrent glioblastoma - a multi-centre UK questionnaire study
abstract: Abstract Background Recurrent glioblastoma (GB) carries a poor prognosis, with physical and cognitive decline significantly affecting patients’ survival and quality of life. Unlike newly-diagnosed GB, there is a paucity of level 1 evidence to guide management, including uncertainty regarding the clinical efficacy and cost-effectiveness of repeat resection prior to second-line chemotherapy. We surveyed UK neuro-oncology specialists to evaluate decision-making practices regarding recurrent GB management and the clinical features influencing them. Methods Between December 2023 and April 2024, a 35-item questionnaire was distributed to consultant neuro-oncologists and neuro-oncology surgeons. Respondents were presented with seven case vignettes simulating first GB recurrences and asked to select suitable treatments, including their single preferred option. We also explored which factors routinely influenced decision-making and extent of multi-disciplinary team (MDT) involvement. Results Thirty-eight responses came from 23 consultant neuro-oncology surgeons and 15 consultant neuro-oncologists across 22 NHS hospitals (response rate 73%). Only 71% routinely re-discussed first recurrence at MDT meetings, with higher re-presentation rates among surgeons. Use of advanced imaging to confirm recurrence was variable: MRI perfusion (74%), MR spectroscopy (53%) and no routine advanced imaging (24%). Best supportive care was often identified as feasible alongside active treatments, particularly with poor prognostic indicators. Factors most commonly influencing re-resection decisions included recurrence interval, performance status, anticipated extent of resection, eloquence and number of tumour foci. Conclusions Substantial inter-clinician variability in preferred management suggests a high degree of clinical equipoise. In this context, there is strong support for randomised trials exploring the clinical efficacy of different management options in recurrent GB, including re- resection surgery.

title: Active learning improves annotation efficiency for colposcopic lesion segmentation under a fixed labeling budget
abstract: Abstract Background: Pixel-level annotation is a major bottleneck in the development of colposcopic lesion segmentation models, particularly when expert annotation resources are limited. This study aimed to determine whether active learning could improve segmentation performance under a fixed annotation budget using a single-center clinical colposcopy dataset. Methods: We implemented a pool-based, batch-mode active learning framework with one warm-start stage and three acquisition rounds. All strategies started with the same 8 labeled images and acquired exactly 15 images per round, resulting in a final labeled pool of 53 images. Six acquisition strategies were compared under the same annotation budget: random sampling, predictive entropy sampling, entropy-MC sampling, K-means representative sampling, Borda-Image, and Borda-Batch. During the retrospective simulation, reference masks in the unlabeled pool were hidden and revealed only after the corresponding images were selected. Models were evaluated on the held-out test set using Dice, intersection-over-union, precision, recall, and the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance. Results: K-means representative sampling achieved the highest Dice score with DeepLabV3+ at 0.5246. Predictive entropy, Borda-Batch, Borda-Image, entropy-MC, and random sampling achieved Dice scores of 0.4879, 0.4755, 0.4642, 0.4559, and 0.3747, respectively. Compared with random sampling, K-means representative sampling improved Dice by 0.1499 under the same labeling budget. Strategy rankings varied across segmentation architectures: K-means representative sampling achieved the highest Dice under DeepLabV3+ and U-Net, whereas predictive entropy achieved the highest Dice under U-Net++. Conclusions: Active learning may improve colposcopic lesion segmentation under a limited annotation budget. In this single-center dataset, feature-space-based representative sampling performed best with DeepLabV3+ and U-Net, while predictive entropy performed best with U-Net++. These findings support further evaluation of active learning in larger, multi-center colposcopy datasets with repeated experiments and external validation.

title: Noninvasive Prediction of HER2 Expression in Bladder Cancer Using a Machine Learning Model Based on Ultrasound Radiomics: Facilitating Precision Screening for ADC Targeted Therapy
abstract: Abstract Objective: To construct and validate an interpretable machine learning model based on ultrasound radiomics for the preoperative prediction of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) expression status in patients with bladder cancer. Methods: This retrospective study included 270 patients with pathologically confirmed bladder cancer, all of whom underwent conventional ultrasound examination preoperatively. Radiomic features were extracted from ultrasound images and subjected to feature selection using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), Spearman correlation analysis, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Four machine learning algorithms, namely, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Random Forest (RF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), were employed to construct predictive models. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. The SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) method was applied for interpretability analysis of the optimal model. Results: A total of 1,288 radiomic features were extracted, of which 5 optimal features were retained for model construction after feature selection. In the test set, the XGBoost model achieved the best performance, with an AUC of 0.817 (95% CI: 0.634–0.999). Conclusion: The interpretable machine learning model based on ultrasound radiomics can preoperatively and noninvasively predict HER2 expression status in bladder cancer, providing valuable reference information for clinical decision-making in individualized ADC-targeted therapy strategies.

title: FZ-VLM: A Two Stage Florence-Zephyr Vision Language Model Framework for Pulmonary Nodule Characterization and Clinical Decision Making
abstract: Abstract Lung cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and Computed Tomography (CT) isa primary imaging tool for screening and follow-up assessment. After pulmonary nodule detection, radiologists manuallyassess anatomical location, diameter, margin characteristics, and attenuation type to support risk assessment and clinicaldecision-making. However, this post-detection workflow is time-consuming and can be affected by inter-observer variability.Existing Artificial Intelligence methods often focus on isolated tasks, which limits their use as a unified and clinically groundedinterpretation framework. This study presents FZ-VLM, a two-stage Florence-Zephyr Vision Language Model framework forunified structured pulmonary nodule characterization in lung CT. The framework uses a fine-tuned Florence-2 model to extractradiological attributes from expert-annotated 2D axial CT slices, while a Zephyr-7B model uses the extracted attributes togenerate nodule descriptions, follow-up recommendations, and longitudinal analysis. A structured Visual Question Answeringdataset containing 8,540 image-prompt-answer triplets was curated from 745 patient cases derived from the National LungScreening Trial. Results showed that the Stage 1 model achieved 77.18% accuracy for anatomical location, 67.96% accuracyfor margin characteristics, and 79.13% accuracy for attenuation type, with a Mean Absolute Error of 2.58 mm for diameterestimation, outperforming evaluated GPT-4-based baselines as well as the human baseline. Expert radiologist evaluation ofStage 2 showed 93.9% accuracy, 98.6% completeness score, 76.1% clinical relevance, and an overall score of 89.5%. Safetyanalysis showed that most outputs were clinically safe, although some follow-up recommendations still required expert review.To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the first two-stage Vision-Language Model framework for structured nodulecharacterization and clinical decision-making system.

title: Timing-Aware Delta-Radiomics After Microwave Ablation of Hepatocellular Carcinoma: An Exploratory MRI Study
abstract: Abstract Background Delta-radiomics may capture treatment-induced imaging changes after thermal ablation, but early post-ablation MRI appearance evolves with time. We explored whether restriction of the first post-ablation MRI to a standardized early follow-up window was associated with different discrimination of local tumor progression (LTP) after complete microwave ablation of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods This retrospective single-center lesion-level study included HCC lesions with initial complete ablation and MRI follow-up. Radiomics features were extracted from pre-ablation tumor and first post-ablation ablation-zone volumes of interest on arterial-phase contrast-enhanced T1-weighted VIBE MRI. Delta features were defined as post-ablation minus pre-ablation values. Time to LTP was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier and Cox models. Twelve-month discrimination was assessed using patient-level grouped cross-validation and patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. Analyses across all post-ablation MRI timings characterized performance in the full evaluable cohort, and a prespecified 20–60-day post-ablation MRI window was examined as a timing-standardized sensitivity analysis. Results In 29 lesions from 28 patients, 12- and 24-month LTP-free survival rates were 0.708 and 0.629, respectively. Tumor size was associated with higher LTP risk. In the 12-month radiomics cohort (24 lesions, 7 events), the clinical model achieved an AUC of 0.731 (95% CI: 0.456–0.970), and adding radiomics across all timings did not improve discrimination. In the 20–60-day subset (21 lesions, 7 events), higher AUC point estimates were observed for pre-ablation plus delta-radiomics (0.888; 95% CI: 0.690–1.000) and clinical plus pre-ablation plus delta-radiomics (0.908; 95% CI: 0.731–1.000). The restricted subset differed from the all-timing cohort by only three lesions. Conclusions Post-ablation MRI timing may contribute to delta-radiomics variability after HCC microwave ablation. The higher 12-month AUC estimates observed in the 20–60-day subset are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as evidence that this window is optimal or that the model is clinically validated. Larger multicenter cohorts with external validation are required.

title: Cross-cohort evaluation of thyroid ultrasound deep learning across different outcome definitions: a duplicate-controlled benchmark
abstract: Abstract Background. Measured performance of thyroid ultrasound artificial intelligence depends on both cohort characteristics and the evaluation endpoint. We assessed frozen models across public cohorts with differing label provenance, separating evaluation against malignancy outcomes from agreement with ultrasound risk categories. Methods. Five backbones were trained on 387 thyroid ultrasound images from 385 public cases (222 papillary thyroid carcinoma, 163 benign) labelled by postoperative diagnosis; 1,332 fine-needle aspiration cytology blocks from the same archive formed a separate benchmark. Exact and perceptual near-duplicates were grouped before image-level partitioning; per-image patient identifiers were unavailable, so patient-level independence could not be confirmed. Frozen models were evaluated on a TN3K subset (n = 1,228; dataset-provided benign/malignant labels) and for concordance with an endpoint derived from radiologist Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) categories in DDTI (n = 637), without retraining or threshold adjustment. Results. On TN3K the ensemble reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.825 (95% confidence interval 0.800–0.849) and ResNet-50 reached 0.888 (0.870–0.904). Against the TI-RADS-derived endpoint, AUROC was 0.477 and 0.437, indicating little agreement with that categorisation. Because cohort, acquisition and endpoint changed together, this contrast cannot be attributed to label definition alone. The cytology benchmark reached AUROC 0.986 (0.970–0.998) against 0.733 for the ultrasound ensemble, a descriptive non-paired contrast. Conclusions. Frozen models performed differently across cohorts differing in acquisition and outcome definition. The findings support explicit reporting of label provenance, cautious interpretation of cross-cohort contrasts, and patient-level external evaluation against a clinically appropriate reference standard.

title: Development and Validation of a Feature-Prompted Deep Learning System for Diagnosing Chronic Atrophic Gastritis Under White-Light Endoscopy
abstract: Abstract Background Chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) is a precancerous condition whose endoscopic detection under white-light endoscopy (WLE) is limited by low sensitivity and high inter-observer variability. We aimed to develop and validate an end-to-end artificial intelligence (AI) system for CAG diagnosis during WLE and compare it with endoscopists of different experience levels. Methods We conducted a single-center retrospective study in which an AI system with three sequential deep learning modules (image quality assessment, anatomical site classification, and atrophy detection) was trained and validated on data from 943 patients. The atrophy detection module used a feature-prompted strategy: segmentation masks were applied to focus the classifier on suspected atrophic regions. The best model was compared with six endoscopists (four intermediate, two senior) on an independent test set, with histopathology as the reference standard. Results The feature-prompted model (DCNN3a-1) reached a sensitivity of 92.4%, specificity of 89.2%, and accuracy of 90.9%. Its accuracy was not significantly different from that of senior endoscopists (90.9% vs. 90.3%, p = 0.738) but was higher than that of intermediate endoscopists (85.6%, p < 0.001) and the overall endoscopist group (87.2%, p < 0.05). Conclusions The AI system achieves expert-level CAG diagnostic performance under WLE. The feature-prompted approach improves accuracy over whole-image classification and may help standardize CAG diagnosis in routine clinical practice.

title: Risk Factors for Cervical Lymph Node Metastasis and a Predictive Model for Lateral Cervical Lymph Node Metastasis in Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma
abstract: Abstract Background: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the most common thyroid malignancy. Although the overall prognosis is favorable, cervical lymph node metastasis (LNM) occurs in a substantial proportion of patients and affects both surgical planning and clinical outcomes. Preoperative ultrasonography remains limited in sensitivity, particularly for occult metastases, and existing predictive tools rarely distinguish between central and lateral compartments. A dedicated model for lateral cervical lymph node metastasis (LC-LNM) is therefore needed. Methods: This single-center retrospective study enrolled 450 patients with newly diagnosed PTC who underwent thyroid surgery between January 2022 and December 2024. Clinicopathological characteristics, BRAF V600E mutation status, preoperative ultrasound features, and surgical data were collected. Variables associated with central lymph node metastasis (CLNM) and LC-LNM were identified by univariate analysis and entered into multivariable binary logistic regression. Model performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit testing, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results: Tumor maximum diameter, BRAF V600E mutation, calcification, and male sex were significantly associated with CLNM. For LC-LNM, tumor diameter, BRAF V600E mutation, calcification, a taller-than-wide shape (aspect ratio >1), tumor laterality (unilateral vs. bilateral), and an indistinct tumor margin were identified as independent correlates. In the resulting LC-LNM model, tumor diameter, BRAF V600E mutation, calcification, and aspect ratio >1 were positive predictors, whereas unilateral lesions and a clear tumor margin were negative predictors. The model showed good fit (Hosmer–Lemeshow P = 0.526) and an AUC of 0.863. Calibration was high (MAE = 0.016; MSE < 0.001; 90th percentile absolute error = 0.055), and DCA indicated net clinical benefit across a threshold probability range of 0.05–0.65. Conclusion: LNM in PTC is associated with a distinct set of clinicopathological factors in the central and lateral compartments. The proposed LC-LNM model integrates readily available preoperative clinical, ultrasound, and molecular variables and may serve as a quantitative adjunct to guide individualized decision-making regarding lateral neck dissection.

title: Oral lichen planus in a patient with neurofibromatosis type 1: the first biopsy- confirmed case report
abstract: Abstract Oral lichen planus co-occurring with neurofibromatosis type 1 is exceptionally rare. A comprehensive literature search revealed no prior reports of biopsy-confirmed OLP in NF1 patients. This report describes the first such case in a 22-year-old woman with familial NF1 confirmed by whole exome sequencing (pathogenic variant: c.2850 + 1delG). The patient presented with a 6-month history of intermittent burning and discomfort in the buccal mucosa during orthodontic treatment. Clinical examination showed bilateral reticular white striae with erythematous erosions on the buccal mucosa, alongside classic NF1 features including multiple café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas. Differential diagnoses such as lichenoid reaction to amalgam, systemic lupus erythematosus, and drug-induced lichenoid reaction were excluded based on the absence of any amalgam restorations, negative serological tests for autoimmune markers (including ANA and anti-dsDNA), lack of systemic symptoms suggestive of SLE, and no history of medications associated with lichenoid reactions. The diagnosis of erosive OLP was clinicopathologic, supported by histopathology revealing band-like lymphocytic infiltrate, basal keratinocyte necrosis, and Civatte bodies. Treatment included incisional biopsy and topical triamcinolone acetonide 0.1%, resulting in complete resolution of lesions and symptoms within one month. No recurrence was observed during the 6-month follow-up, and orthodontic treatment progressed uneventfully. This case documents the first biopsy-confirmed erosive OLP in an NF1 patient, emphasizing the importance of routine oral screening and multidisciplinary management given the potential risk of malignant transformation in OLP (approximately 1–2%).

This case documents the first biopsy-confirmed erosive OLP in an NF1 patient, emphasizing the importance of routine oral screening and multidisciplinary management given the potential risk of malignant transformation in OLP (approximately 1–2%).

title: Anti-Ku antibody-positive interstitial lung disease with and without established systemic autoimmune disease: a descriptive study
abstract: Abstract Background Although anti-Ku antibodies have been reported in various connective tissue diseases (CTDs), data on the clinical characteristics of anti-Ku antibody-positive interstitial lung disease (ILD) remain limited. This study investigated the clinical, radiological, and pathological features of anti-Ku antibody-positive ILD. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 13 patients with anti-Ku antibody-positive ILD at our institution between 2018 and 2025. Data on baseline characteristics, imaging, pathology, treatment, and outcomes were collected. Results Seven patients (53.8%) were diagnosed with CTDs. CTD was present in idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (IIM; n = 2), systemic sclerosis (SSc), IIM with SSc overlap, microscopic polyangiitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjögren’s syndrome (n = 1, each). ILD preceded the diagnosis of CTDs in two of these patients. Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) was the most frequent pattern (n = 5, 38.5%) on chest computed tomography, followed by usual interstitial pneumonia (probable UIP, n = 4, 30.8%). On lung histopathology, the patterns were heterogeneous; fibrotic NSIP and NSIP with organizing pneumonia were each observed in two patients, whereas UIP features were present in four patients. During the observation period (mean 51.7 ± 32.1 months), four patients developed progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF). Among the seven patients in whom any radiological and/or pathological UIP feature was present, four (57.1%) developed PPF or experienced acute exacerbation. Conclusions Anti-Ku antibody-positive ILD shows a heterogeneous clinical spectrum that includes both CTD-associated and non-CTD phenotypes. Progressive fibrotic disease was observed in both groups, while radiological and/or pathological UIP features may help identify patients at increased risk of disease progression.

title: Spatial artificial intelligence in gastric endoscopy for premalignant lesions and early gastric cancer: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence in gastric endoscopy increasingly produces spatial outputs to localize abnormal mucosa and define lesion extent, yet their clinical validity is uncertain. We conducted a task-specific systematic review nested within a prospectively registered parent review and identified 39 study families evaluating localization, segmentation, boundary identification, or margin delineation in gastric premalignant lesions and early gastric cancer. Most studies assessed segmentation on stored images. Histopathology often confirmed diagnosis, but spatial references were usually expert-defined endoscopic masks rather than pathology-registered boundaries. Only three studies reported patient-disjoint internal testing, six external validation, six a prospective component, and two live spatial evaluations; one study showed procedure-altering biopsy guidance. Dice, IoU, boundary, and margin measures were heterogeneous and were not pooled. Spatial AI has moved toward clinically relevant mapping and margin assessment, but stronger reference standards and validation during endoscopy are needed before these outputs can support procedural decisions.

title: Neutrophil percentage-to-albumin ratio and late gadolinium enhancement in clinically suspected myocarditis: a multicentre retrospective study
abstract: Abstract Background Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging identifies myocardial involvement in myocarditis and carries prognostic weight. The neutrophil percentage-to-albumin ratio (NPAR) combines neutrophil predominance with serum albumin, a negative acute-phase reactant. Whether NPAR is associated with LGE, and whether it adds information to its individual components and to routinely available clinical data, is unknown. Methods This retrospective observational study included 1,055 adults with clinically suspected myocarditis who underwent CMR at seven tertiary cardiovascular centres in Türkiye between October 2022 and September 2025. All studies were reviewed centrally by three cardiovascular radiologists blinded to clinical and laboratory data (Fleiss' κ = 0.83). Variables significant on univariable analysis (p < 0.10) were entered into multivariable logistic regression models, the shape of the association was examined using restricted cubic splines, and the incremental value of NPAR over the clinical and laboratory model was assessed using discrimination and reclassification metrics. Results LGE was present in 285 patients (27.0%). NPAR was higher in the LGE-positive group [1.65 (1.40–1.92) vs. 1.29 (1.02–1.55); p < 0.001]. In the multivariable model, NPAR remained independently associated with LGE positivity (adjusted odds ratio per 1 standard deviation 4.381, 95% confidence interval 3.248–5.907; p < 0.001), and the Nagelkerke R² rose from 0.157 to 0.387. Restricted cubic spline analysis showed a positive association across the observed range with evidence of non-linearity (p = 0.013). Adding NPAR increased the area under the curve of the model from 0.728 (0.687–0.768) to 0.839 (0.806–0.872) (difference 0.111; p < 0.001), with an integrated discrimination improvement of 0.194 (0.133–0.251) and a continuous net reclassification improvement of 0.843 (0.674–1.011), both p < 0.001. As a single marker, NPAR yielded an area under the curve of 0.750 (0.718–0.782) at a cut-off of 1.43, discriminating LGE better than either constituent (both p < 0.0001). Conclusions In clinically suspected myocarditis, NPAR was independently associated with CMR-defined LGE positivity, discriminated LGE better than either of its own components, and provided significant incremental discrimination and reclassification over a clinical and laboratory model. NPAR may serve as a low-cost adjunctive marker where access to CMR is constrained.

title: Early- Versus Late-Onset Fetal Growth Restriction: Clinical Features, Placental Histopathology, and Risk Factor Analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a critical adverse pregnancy complication that significantly contributes to adverse perinatal prognosis, and its clinical manifestations, pathological mechanisms and prognostic impacts vary greatly according to the gestational age of onset. Early-onset and late-onset FGR differ substantially in disease severity and underlying etiologies, to date, few studies have systematically compared the clinical characteristics and placental histopathological lesions of early- and late-onset FGR. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the clinical profiles and placental pathological changes between the two FGR subtypes and further screen key risk factors for early-onset FGR, so as to provide pathological and clinical evidence for the early identification and stratified clinical management of early-onset FGR. Methods Our cohort investigation encompassed 461 singleton pregnancies, including FGR, stratified by gestational age at diagnosis into early- and late-onset groups. Maternal demographics, pregnancy complications, delivery outcomes, Doppler parameters, and placental pathology were contrasted across groups. Multivariate regression characterized risk factors for early-onset FGR was constructed. Results Early-onset FGR was associated with significantly lower birth weight, higher preterm birth (PB) rates, worse perinatal outcomes, and more severe maternal vascular malperfusion (MVM) in placental lesions compared to late-onset FGR ( p < 0.05). Relevant risk factors associated with early-onset FGR included autoimmune disease, thyroid disorder, intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), and abnormal umbilical artery Doppler, with a particularly strong association with preeclampsia. Conclusion Early-onset FGR is characterized by greater disease severity and is strongly linked to maternal systemic conditions, placental vascular insufficiency, and aberrant Doppler hemodynamics. Early-onset FGR is fundamentally a placenta-mediated vascular disorder, compounded by secondary inflammatory activation and maternal systemic dysfunction. Targeted management of these risk factors may improve perinatal outcomes.

title: An Automated, Contamination-Controlled VQA Benchmark for Evaluating Vision-Language Models on 3D Oncology Imaging
abstract: Abstract Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly applied to medical imaging, yet public benchmarks may reward memorization over perception: their images and questions can enter pretraining corpora, and many items remain answerable from question text alone. We present an automated, agent-driven pipeline that builds multiple-choice benchmarks directly from paired private radiology reports and three-dimensional oncology imaging. It generates two complementary question types: schema-driven items populated deterministically from established reporting frameworks, and report-derived items verified against the source text. Because the source reports are private and single-institution, the resulting questions cannot have entered any model’s pretraining data, controlling instance-level contamination by construction. We applied the pipeline to four oncology cohorts (liver CT, liver MRI, lung CT and brain MRI; 2,509 cases and 33,870 questions) and evaluated five contemporary VLMs zero-shot. Accuracies ranged from 0.28 to 0.81 and no model was reliable across cohorts. Replacing the image with a blank input changed accuracy little for the highest-scoring models, and on schema-driven brain questions frontier models scored 0.17–0.19 higher on public than on matched private imaging. The benchmark thus separates image-dependent performance from question-text and dataset-familiarity effects, and the released pipeline lets institutions regenerate it on their own reports and images.

title: Non-contrast CT Radiomics Combined with Clinical Features for Predicting Secondary Sepsis in Severe Acute Pancreatitis
abstract: Abstract Objective: To evaluate models based on non-contrast computed tomography (CT) radiomics and early clinical data for predicting secondary sepsis in patients with severe acute pancreatitis (SAP). Methods: This retrospective single-centre study included 253 patients with SAP admitted to the Second Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University between January 2021 and December 2025. Patients were allocated to a training cohort (n = 202) and an internal test cohort (n = 51) using an approximately 8:2 stratified random split. The first eligible non-contrast abdominal CT examination performed within 1 week of symptom onset was used to delineate the pancreas and contiguous peripancreatic inflammatory lesions. A total of 107 radiomics features were extracted using PyRadiomics. All candidate predictors were obtained before a prespecified prediction time point. Feature standardisation, selection and model development were conducted exclusively in the training cohort, and the training-derived classification thresholds were applied unchanged to the test cohort. Logistic regression was used to develop a clinical signature, a radiomics signature and a combined nomogram. Discrimination, calibration and clinical utility were assessed using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration curves, the Hosmer-Lemeshow test and decision curve analysis. Results: Secondary sepsis occurred in 54 patients in the training cohort and 14 in the test cohort. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression retained eight radiomics features. In the training cohort, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.858 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.806-0.909) for the clinical signature, 0.675 (95% CI, 0.587-0.762) for the radiomics signature and 0.867 (95% CI, 0.814-0.919) for the combined nomogram. In the test cohort, the corresponding AUCs were 0.699 (95% CI, 0.542-0.855), 0.697 (95% CI, 0.550-0.843) and 0.732 (95% CI, 0.593-0.870), respectively. The combined nomogram achieved a sensitivity of 0.929 and a negative predictive value of 0.955, whereas the clinical signature achieved a specificity of 0.757. The radiomics signature showed no evidence of lack of fit in either cohort (P = 0.508 and P = 0.306). Conclusions: A radiomics signature derived from non-contrast CT may provide complementary information for risk stratification of secondary sepsis in SAP. The combined nomogram showed the highest AUC and a high negative predictive value in the internal test cohort, but its performance and calibration require confirmation and recalibration in larger external multicentre cohorts.

title: Clinical Observation of CD7-Directed CAR-T cell Therapy in Relapsed/Refractory Mixed Phenotype Acute Leukaemia
abstract: Abstract Mixed phenotype acute leukaemia (MPAL) currently lacks a specific target for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, and effective treatment options for patients with relapsed/refractory disease remain limited. CD7-directed CAR-T cell therapy has achieved high complete remission rates with a favourable safety profile in patients with relapsed/refractory T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (R/R T-ALL). Given that CD7 is expressed on leukaemic blasts in a subset of patients with MPAL, we therefore used humanised CD7-directed CAR-T (hCD7 CAR-T) cells as salvage therapy in selected patients with relapsed/refractory MPAL (R/R MPAL) and evaluated the safety and efficacy of this approach. Between April 2024 to December 2025, seven patients with R/R MPAL who received hCD7 CAR-T therapy were retrospectively analysed. All patients had CD7 expression > 80% on leukaemic cells by flow cytometry. CAR-T cells were generated through transduction with a second-generation CAR lentiviral vector encoding CD3ζ-4-1BB. Before CAR-T infusion, patients received a lymphodepletion regimen based on fludarabine and/or cyclophosphamide. CAR-T cells were cultured for 5–8 days and then infused into patients. Treatment efficacy was assessed on day 30 after infusion. Minimal residual disease (MRD) was evaluated using FCM and quantitative PCR methods. Extramedullary lesions were assessed by PET/CT, CT, or ultrasonography. Patients were followed regularly until 30 April 2026. The median age was 33 years (range 18–70). Five patients had bone marrow haematological relapse (including 3 patients with extramedullary lesions), 2 patients had bone marrow MRD-positive disease, and 1 patient had relapsed after transplantation. The median infused CAR-T cell dose was 5.0 × 10⁵/kg (range 1.0–9.0 × 10⁵/kg). The major treatment-related adverse event was cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and all cases were Grade 1. Five patients received supportive treatment, 1 patient received supportive treatment and corticosteroids, and 1 patient received supportive treatment, corticosteroids, siltuximab, and etoposide. Symptoms improved in all patients, and no treatment-related mortality occurred. At day 30 after CAR-T infusion, 6 patients achieved complete remission (CR), including 1 patient with MRD-positive CR, resulting in a complete remission rate of 85.7%. One patient showed no response. The median follow-up duration was 8.3 months (range 4.7–24.4). All patients underwent bridging allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) 5–8 weeks after CAR-T therapy. Five patients achieved continuous complete remission (CCR), with remission durations of 24.4, 12.5, 6.0, 5.2, and 4.7 months, respectively. One patient relapsed at 7 months post-transplant, and one non-responder patient experienced bone marrow haematological relapse and multiple extramedullary relapses at 6.9 months post-transplant and died of disease progression. In conclusion, hCD7 CAR-T therapy demonstrated a high CR rate of 85.7% and a favourable safety profile in patients with CD7-positive R/R MPAL. Durable remissions were achievable with bridging allo-HSCT, though patients failing to respond had a poor prognosis.

title: Comparative detection performance of different imaging modalities in suspected cardiac sarcoidosis: A systematic review and network meta-analysis
abstract: Abstract Background The optimal imaging modality for detecting cardiac sarcoidosis remains uncertain, since direct comparative data are largely limited to single tracer pairs. The aim of the present study was to estimate and rank the diagnostic detection performance of positron emission tomography (PET), cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), and conventional scintigraphy modalities in suspected cardiac sarcoidosis through a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA). Methods PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to June 2026 for studies directly comparing at least two imaging modalities. A frequentist random-effect NMA was conducted with detection rate (DR) as primary outcome, 18 F-FDG PET/CT as reference, and effect sizes expressed as risk differences (RDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Node-splitting and sensitivity analyses were applied to assess consistency and rank stability. Results Ten studies (n = 430 patients or lesions) met inclusion criteria, forming a network of nine modalities. CMR with late gadolinium enhancement (CMR-LGE) yielded the highest DR (RD 0.18 versus 18 F-FDG PET/CT; 95% CI, 0.11 to 0.25), followed by 68 Ga-DOTANOC PET/CT (RD 0.11; 95% CI, − 0.09 to 0.30); 18 F-FLT PET/CT was essentially equivalent to the reference (RD 0.00; 95% CI, − 0.23 to 0.24). 67 Ga scintigraphy yielded the lowest DR (RD − 0.73; 95% CI, − 0.82 to − 0.65). Four modalities differed significantly from 18 F-FDG PET/CT (CMR-LGE above the reference, and 67 Ga scintigraphy, 99m Tc-MIBI SPECT, and T2w-CMR below). Conclusion Our findings suggest that CMR-LGE and 68 Ga-DOTANOC PET/CT may yield a higher DR than 18 F-FDG PET/CT, while conventional radionuclide techniques appear comparatively limited. Trial registration: INPLASY (INPLASY202630093)

title: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis Presenting as Refractory Bilateral Lower Extremity Edema: Rapid Resolution After Unilateral Biportal Endoscopic Surgery—A Case Report and Literature Review
abstract: Abstract Purpose Bilateral lower extremity edema is a common clinical symptom, often caused by cardiac, hepatic, renal, or venous disorders. However, the etiology of some refractory cases remains occult, and in such instances, lumbar spinal stenosis—a spinal etiology—is easily overlooked. Prolonged lower extremity edema secondary to lumbar spinal stenosis has rarely been reported in the literature, and the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms remain elusive.This case presents a unique instance where severe L4/5 lumbar spinal stenosis manifested solely as a five-year history of refractory bilateral calf edema, occurring in the complete absence of low back pain, sciatica, or neurogenic claudication. Notably, the edema resolved rapidly and completely following unilateral biportal endoscopic (UBE) decompression, providing direct in vivo evidence that stenosis-related edema is reversible after neural decompression. By documenting this rare presentation and its dramatic treatment response, this report aims to (1) raise awareness of a treatable spinal etiology in cryptogenic bilateral edema, (2) advocate for lumbar MRI as a screening modality, even in patients lacking overt spinal symptoms, and (3) provide mechanistic insights regarding epidural venous plexus compression and neurogenic inflammation, thereby expanding the etiological spectrum of lower extremity edema. Case Presentation A 76-year-old female presented with a five-year history of persistent symmetrical pitting edema of both calves, in the absence of low back pain, radicular pain, or motor deficits. Routine medical workup was unremarkable, with cardiac, hepatic, renal, and vascular etiologies excluded. Multiple therapeutic trials involving volume depletion strategies and diuretics proved ineffective. Subsequently, lumbar MRI and CT demonstrated severe lumbar spinal stenosis at the L4/L5 level. Results Following L4/5 unilateral biportal endoscopic (UBE) decompressive surgery (partial laminectomy with ligamentum flavum resection and central/lateral recess decompression under general anesthesia),bilateral calf edema markedly subsided on the first postoperative day and completely resolved by postoperative day 9.A repeat lower extremity ultrasound showed resolution of subcutaneous soft tissue edema in both calves.At the 4-week follow-up,no recurrence of lower extremity edema was observed. Conclusion This case illustrates that lumbar spinal stenosis represents a rare but reversible cause of refractory lower extremity edema. Proposed mechanisms may involve impaired venous return due to compression of the epidural venous plexus and potentially neurogenic inflammation. Lumbar MRI should be considered a screening tool for unexplained, refractory lower extremity edema. The UBE technique, as a minimally invasive and precise decompression approach, provides an effective treatment option for such patients and broadens the clinical understanding of the etiological spectrum of lower extremity edema.

title: Ultrasound-based deep learning-derived radiomics for preoperative prediction of sentinel lymph node metastasis in invasive breast cancer: a two-center retrospective study
abstract: Abstract Background Preoperative assessment of sentinel lymph node (SLN) metastasis may support individualized axillary management in patients with invasive breast cancer (IBC). We developed and externally validated a deep learning-derived ultrasound radiomics model for predicting SLN metastasis. Methods This retrospective two-center study included 246 patients with pathologically confirmed IBC. Center A provided 194 patients (93 with SLN metastasis), who were divided into training (n = 155) and internal test (n = 39) cohorts; 52 patients from Center B (20 with SLN metastasis) constituted an external validation cohort. Deep features were extracted from preoperative ultrasound images using a ResNet50 architecture. Feature selection was performed in the training cohort, and a gradient boosting decision tree classifier was developed. Discrimination was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis; decision curve analysis was performed as an exploratory assessment of net benefit. Results Twenty-two deep learning-derived features were retained for model development. The model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.734 (95% CI, 0.655–0.813) in the training cohort, 0.761 (95% CI, 0.601–0.920) in the internal test cohort, and 0.742 (95% CI, 0.598–0.886) in the external validation cohort. In the external cohort, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were 0.769, 0.650, 0.844, 0.722, and 0.794, respectively. Decision curves are reported as exploratory analyses and do not establish clinical utility. Conclusion A deep learning-derived ultrasound radiomics model showed moderate and relatively consistent discrimination for SLN metastasis across the development and external validation cohorts. These findings support further evaluation of the model as an adjunctive preoperative risk-stratification tool; prospective validation in larger and more diverse populations is required before clinical implementation.

title: Functional Transopercular Transinsular Mesialtemporal Surgical Corridor in Mesial Temporal-Insular Tumors
abstract: Abstract Background Transcortical approaches to insula tumours have gained popularity in the recent years alongside with the widespread use of awake surgical techniques and intraoperative neuromonitoring developments. The transopercular transinsular mesialtemporal surgical corridor offers a functional approach for accessing mesial temporal-insular lesions. Case presentations and Surgical technique: A 36-year-old woman who presented with epileptic seizures and was found to have a left temporo-insular lesion on MRI. The technique performed through the temporal opercula after cortical mapping for the relevant cognitive functions – language, cognition and motor. Preoperative cortical mapping with navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation and/or functional MRI provide significant preoperative information to inform intraoperative cortical mapping. After skeletonizing the M3 branches, the approach follows a surgical structural corridor between arcuate fasciculus, superior longitudinal fasciculus system, fronto-aslant tract, and corticospinal tract superiorly and medially, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus medially, uncinate fasciculus anteriorly, inferior and medial longitudinal fasciculus laterally and optic radiations posteriorly, reaching the mesial temporal region – uncus and hippocampal formation. At subcortical level, the boundaries of this structural corridor are functionally identified with the appropriate intraoperative testing. Asleep intraoperative testing focuses on motor evoked potentials (MEPs) mapping and monitoring using either high frequency (HFS) or low frequency (LFS) techniques, somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) and/or cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEP). Awake intraoperative mapping and monitoring relies on the above mentioned techniques and temporary cognitive function disruption using language, social and motor cognition tasks - with either HFS or LFS techniques. Conclusion The functional transopercular transinsular mesialtemporal surgical corridor enables maximal safe resection of tumors extending to the uncus and hippocampal formation while preserving functional cortical-subcortical structures and minimizing vascular morbidity.

title: Rare bone metastasis from primary hepatic angiosarcoma: A case report and literature review
abstract: Abstract Background Primary hepatic angiosarcoma (PHA) is a rare, aggressive vascular endothelial soft-tissue sarcoma comprising < 2% of all soft-tissue sarcomas. Unlike cutaneous or breast angiosarcoma, PHA is significantly rarer and associated with a dismal prognosis (median survival, ~ 6 months). While Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (KMS) is the most frequent hematologic complication, bone metastasis is exceedingly rare. Case presentation We report a 67-year-old man admitted with fatigue for two months and newly discovered thrombocytopenia. Comprehensive imaging and biopsy confirmed hepatic angiosarcoma with bone metastasis. Following contraindication exclusion, he received combination chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy. Interval abdominal CT showed stable disease without obvious tumor enlargement, though refractory thrombocytopenia persisted throughout the treatment course. Conclusion PHA typically presents with nonspecific, insidious symptoms overlapping with chronic liver disease, often resulting in delayed diagnosis. While bone marrow metastasis is rare, early bone marrow aspiration should be considered in patients with thrombocytopenia as the presenting feature. Currently, no definitive treatment regimen exists; management should be individualized and dynamically adjusted.

title: Vosoritide Treatment Does Not Change the Robust Bone Phenotype of Children with Achondroplasia
abstract: Abstract Background Vosoritide is an FDA-approved bone-lengthening treatment for children with achondroplasia, the most common form of disproportionate short stature. Whether this bone-lengthening treatment provides commensurate changes in cross-sectional morphology, to ensure bone strength is not deleteriously affected, is unknown. Thus, we sought to characterize the bone morphological parameters of children with achondroplasia on vosoritide using measurements of the second metacarpal. Methods This study included deidentified anteroposterior hand/wrist radiographs from 30 children with achondroplasia (13 males, 17 females; age 5.8 − 11.1 years). Proprietary hand films were collected at screening (pre-treatment) and at 5 years on treatment. Measurements included second metacarpal length and midshaft width, cortical thickness, robustness (total area/length) and cortical area, which correlates with strength. Measurements were compared between the two time-points via non-parametric Wilcoxon tests, and with 378 radiographs from 114 average-statured controls who did not receive vosoritide treatment (61 males, 53 females; age 6 − 16 years) via Kruskal-Wallis tests (p < 0.05). Results Compared to average-stature controls, children with achondroplasia exhibited a more robust bone phenotype (p < 0.001). After 5 years of vosoritide treatment, children with achondroplasia demonstrated increased metacarpal length and cortical area compared to their own baseline values (all p < 0.05). No sex differences were observed. Conclusions Altogether, increases in metacarpal total area and cortical area kept up with increases in metacarpal length over the course of 5 years of vosoritide treatment. As the bones lengthened, subperiosteal expansion continued at a pace which maintained robustness, allowing the bone to remain strong. This preliminary data suggests that vosoritide did not alter the naturally robust bone phenotype of children with achondroplasia. Clinical trial registration Clinical trial registry: ClinicalTrials.gov. Clinical trial numbers: NCT02055157 (registered January 13, 2014) and NCT02724228 (registered January 26, 2016).

title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Shoulder Pseudodislocation Secondary to Calcific Tendinopathy: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Shoulder pseudodislocation is a rare clinical condition. Imaging examination shows displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid, while the osseous anatomical alignment of the joint remains intact. This article reports a 52-year-old female patient with a long history of rotator cuff calcific tendinopathy. The patient presented with recurrent chronic dull shoulder pain, recently aggravated pain, and restricted shoulder movement. Shoulder radiography revealed a dislocation-like appearance of the glenohumeral joint, calcified lesions located at the superolateral humeral head, and widening of the glenohumeral joint space. Given the absence of shoulder trauma, immediate manual reduction was not performed. Further multimodal imaging examinations including CT and MRI were completed, and the patient was finally diagnosed with shoulder pseudodislocation secondary to calcific tendinitis. CT demonstrated calcified deposits at the superolateral humeral head, whereas MRI showed supraspinatus tendon injury, extensive periarticular soft tissue edema, and glenohumeral joint capsular effusion. The patient underwent arthroscopic calcified lesion debridement combined with subacromial decompression. Postoperative radiographic reexamination at day 1 and 2 weeks revealed significant reduction of calcified lesions and gradual recovery of the abnormally widened glenohumeral joint space. Postoperative follow-up showed nearly complete relief of shoulder pain, full recovery of shoulder forward flexion, external rotation and abduction, and unremarkable limitation in daily activities. Based on this rare case, the present study aims to summarize the imaging characteristics and diagnostic and therapeutic strategies of shoulder pseudodislocation secondary to calcific tendinitis, to distinguish soft tissue-induced pseudodislocation from traumatic true shoulder dislocation, and to avoid unnecessary closed reduction. This study provides clinical evidence for preoperative imaging evaluation and minimally invasive surgical treatment of similar rare secondary shoulder lesions.
